title: `kubectl describe pod` probe host is empty
body:
### What happened?

Using `kubectl describe po xxx` to show pod probe info, when the probe host is empty, there is no default value showed in the output, like below, so this PR add the default value.
```
    State:          Running
      Started:      Thu, 19 Dec 2024 15:25:42 +0800
    Ready:          False
    Restart Count:  0
    ...
    Liveness:       http-get http://:8080/healthz delay=0s timeout=5s period=10s #success=1 #failure=3
```

### What did you expect to happen?

When the host not set, add the default value `localhost`.
```
    Liveness:       http-get http://:8080/healthz delay=0s timeout=5s period=10s #success=1 #failure=3
    ======== to below
    Liveness:       http-get http://localhost:8080/healthz delay=0s timeout=5s period=10s #success=1 #failure=3
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.7.9
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          timeoutSeconds: 5

```
`kubectl apply -f xxx.yaml && kubectl describe po xxx` will reproduce this issue.

### Anything else we need to know?

Issue tested in 1.31.

### Kubernetes version

1.31

# Kubernetes 系统组件预留资源：确保 kubernetes 组件（如 kubelet）有足够资源运行

经过验证，使用这位朋友的办法能解决这个报错：赞

下面的缩进有问题，请看链接里的详细缩进

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/127316#issuecomment-2348662766

To resolve the issue I have edited the kubeadm-config configmap within kube-system to add the ControlPlaneKubeletLocalMode flag as below：

apiVersion: v1
data:
  ClusterConfiguration: |
    apiServer:
      extraArgs:
      - name: authorization-mode
        value: Node,RBAC
    apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta4
    caCertificateValidityPeriod: 87600h0m0s
    certificateValidityPeriod: 8760h0m0s
    certificatesDir: /etc/kubernetes/pki
    clusterName: kubernetes
    controlPlaneEndpoint: kubernetes.cluster.local:6443
    controllerManager: {}
    dns: {}
    encryptionAlgorithm: RSA-2048
    etcd:
      local:
        dataDir: /var/lib/etcd
++    featureGates:
++      ControlPlaneKubeletLocalMode: true
    imageRepository: registry.k8s.io


After adding the flag and upgrading a control-plane node the /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf file is updated so the server field connects to the host itself rather then the cluster vip address.

apiVersion: v1
clusters:
- cluster:
    certificate-authority-data: 
      CLUSTER-CERTIFICATE-REMOVED
--    server: https://kubernetes.cluster.local:6443
++    server: https://10.0.0.12:6443
  name: default-cluster
contexts:
- context:
    cluster: default-cluster
    namespace: default
    user: default-auth
  name: default-context
current-context: default-context
kind: Config
preferences: {}
users:
- name: default-auth
  user:
    client-certificate: /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem
    client-key: /var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem


So if a controller has already been upgraded and is now failing, changing the server address within kubelet.conf will return the node to service and adding the flag will make it permanent for future upgrades.

I don't know what the official or recommended fix will be but this is working well for me.
The root cause is explained in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cluster-api/pull/10947: this is https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123905.

title: The container_memory_working_set_bytes indicator corresponding to a container has three records.
body:
### What happened?

When the container_memory_working_set_bytes indicator is queried through the Cadvisor interface, three data records exist in the same container, and the corresponding IDs are nested. Why?
```

title: Empty annotation removes all existing and valid annotations
body:
### What happened?

When creating a resource (e.g. a Service) with annotations the annotations are all removed when one of them has an empty value. The same happens on update.
It happens in our production environment as well as locally on minikube so I don't expect anything we deployed there to interfere with it.

### What did you expect to happen?

Applying the resource should fail on empty values

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a Service (notice the empty `baz` annotation)

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service
  annotations:
    foo: bar
    baz:
spec:
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: MyApp
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 9376
```

Apply it

```
kubectl apply -f my-service.yaml
```

Retrieve it
```
kubectl get service my-service -o yaml
```

The service also lacks the `foo` annotation
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  annotations:
    kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: |
      {"apiVersion":"v1","kind":"Service","metadata":{"annotations":{},"name":"my-service","namespace":"default"},"spec":{"ports":[{"port":80,"protocol":"TCP","targetPort":9376}],"selector":{"app.kubernetes.io/name":"MyApp"}}}
  creationTimestamp: "2024-12-12T12:16:24Z"

  namespace: default
  resourceVersion: "1776057"
  uid: a947a42c-a922-4f67-8103-c88dbb814004

status:

```
  

### Anything else we need to know?

This happens with `kubectl apply` but also with `helm install`

I also am able to reproduce it.

It certainly is a surprising result.

A few things I notice when trying to reproduce it:

1. The `-v9` output shows that kubectl doesn't send either annotation in the request.

2. Server side apply seems to not have the problem:
```
~/projects/ktest/k-129176 $ kubectl apply -f svc.yaml --server-side
service/my-service serverside-applied
~/projects/ktest/k-129176 $ kubectl get svc my-service -o yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  annotations:
    baz: ""
    foo: bar
  creationTimestamp: "2024-12-16T23:37:48Z"
  name: my-service
  namespace: default
  resourceVersion: "162716"
  uid: 0857690a-2da1-43ad-b5db-8437946e79ff
spec:
  clusterIP: 10.96.9.210
  clusterIPs:
  - 10.96.9.210
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  ipFamilies:
  - IPv4
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ports:
  - port: 80
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 9376
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: MyApp
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: ClusterIP
status:
  loadBalancer: {}
```

/triage accepted
/sig cli

Annotations are string maps and both of key and value must be string. [GetModifiedConfiguration](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3ec97a445f036a38bfec6291dee661954138bac9/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/util/apply.go#L78) function calls `NestedStringMap` and this function fails when there is a non-string value in [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3ec97a445f036a38bfec6291dee661954138bac9/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/unstructured/helpers.go#L197-L201). Consequently, all the annotations in the object are cleared up, since we couldn't extract the annotations in the object.

It would be better to propagate this error to the user for better experience. However, GetAnnotations functions interface is `GetAnnotations() map[string]string` which does not contain error.

I tried `bar: ""` instead of nil and it worked.

I think, always using `--server-side` in lieu of `client-side` in apply is still the best recommended path.
@brianpursley @ardaguclu Can I work on this issue? Would it be better to propagate the error to the users in this case?
/assign
@ali-hamza-noor This requires significant changes in the code base and it is not possible that we can change the signature of function to return the error.

One possibility is to do additional validation specifically within kubectl to make sure labels and annotations are well-formed and don't specify `null` - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/129255 is an example of that

The issue with that approach is that it will break commands like `kubectl create`, `kubectl replace`, and `kubectl apply --server-side` which currently turn `null` label and annotation values into empty strings:

`more nullannotation.yaml`
> ```yaml
> apiVersion: v1
> kind: ConfigMap
> metadata:
>   name: test
>   annotations:
>     foo: "x"
>     bar:
> data:
>   key: value
> ```

`kubectl create -f nullannotation.yaml -o yaml`:
> ```yaml
> apiVersion: v1
> data:
>   key: value
> kind: ConfigMap
> metadata:
>   annotations:
>     bar: ""
>     foo: x
>   creationTimestamp: "2024-12-17T15:32:05Z"
>   name: test
>   namespace: default
>   resourceVersion: "288"
>   uid: a6ccf114-7a6f-442f-b36e-f240c81376c0
> ```

`kubectl replace -f nullannotation.yaml -o yaml`:
> ```yaml
> apiVersion: v1
> data:
>   key: value
> kind: ConfigMap
> metadata:
>   annotations:
>     bar: ""
>     foo: x
>   creationTimestamp: "2024-12-17T15:36:10Z"
>   name: test
>   namespace: default
>   resourceVersion: "353"
>   uid: f8669ddf-900c-4ea5-ac74-5e6726b69357
> ```

`kubectl apply --server-side -f nullannotation.yaml -o yaml`:
> ```yaml
> apiVersion: v1
> data:
>   key: value
> kind: ConfigMap
> metadata:
>   annotations:
>     bar: ""
>     foo: x
>   creationTimestamp: "2024-12-17T15:32:28Z"
>   name: test
>   namespace: default
>   resourceVersion: "295"
>   uid: de32754a-44bb-44e0-97ef-2382396e422c
> ```

Only client-side apply (or things which try to set client-side apply annotations with `--set-config`) have this issue where they drop all other annotations:
`kubectl apply -f nullannotation.yaml -o yaml`:
> ```yaml
> apiVersion: v1
> data:
>   key: value
> kind: ConfigMap
> metadata:
>   annotations:
>     kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration: |
>       {"apiVersion":"v1","data":{"key":"value"},"kind":"ConfigMap","metadata":{"annotations":{},"name":"test","namespace":"default"}}
>   creationTimestamp: "2024-12-17T15:32:51Z"
>   name: test
>   namespace: default
>   resourceVersion: "302"
>   uid: 5b73bc45-5a09-4969-b5d4-9d295cd81a8d
> ```


Another possibility is to coerce null values to empty strings, to match what create / replace / server-side-apply do. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/129257 does that.

nodes.title: Coerce null label and annotation values to empty string
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adjusts unstructured label and annotation accessors to tolerate / coerce null values in the maps to empty string values.

This matches json decoding behavior and server-side behavior if those values were sent to the server.

/sig api-machinery

Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129176

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

title: draplugin.PublishResources() only supports enumerating resources in a single slice
body:
### What happened?

I wanted to publish multiple resource slices within the same pool, but there was no easy way to do this with the recommended helper library.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the API to `draplugin.PublishResources()` to take a list of ResourceSlices, similar to the call to `resourceslice.Update()` that it wraps. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This is an oversight. Ideally we should fix this quickly and backport to v1.32.1 for DRA drivers targeting 1.32.

Should we modify the original API interface or add a new one? 🤔 
like this: 
`PublishMultipleResources(ctx context.Context, resourcesList []Resources) error`

We can just change the existing Go API. It means that DRA drivers need to be updated when bumping their dependencies from v1.32.0 to v1.32.1, but that's okay: the k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation module has version v0.32.0 resp. v0.32.1, i.e. no API stability guarantee.

Got it, I'd like to try this.
/assign

> We can just change the existing Go API. It means that DRA drivers need to be updated when bumping their dependencies from v1.32.0 to v1.32.1, but that's okay: the k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation module has version v0.32.0 resp. v0.32.1, i.e. no API stability guarantee.

then why is it in staging if there is no guarantee between minors?

At least we should document it

Between 0.32.0 and 0.33.0? It's normal Go practice that there there is no API stability for 0.x releases. While we strive for more stability in staging repos, we also have always reserved the right to change APIs if needed. This one falls into that category.

Actually, it's even [documented explicitly already](https://github.com/kubernetes/dynamic-resource-allocation?tab=readme-ov-file#compatibility)! :smile:

Or did you mean between patch releases (major.minor.patch), i.e. 0.32.0 and 0.32.1?

While unusual, "no compatibility guarantees" also extends to patch releases.

> There are NO compatibility guarantees for this repository, yet. It is in direct support of Kubernetes, so branches will track Kubernetes and be compatible with that repo.

Kubernetes compatibility rules are much stricter as you can see in the backport rules, https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-release/cherry-picks.md

I don't see anything in that document about "don't break APIs".

I fully understand that this would be surprising and that it might not be important enough for a backport, but in this case forgetting to update that API in 1.32.0 is the bug that we want to fix.

Okay, let's not backport.

DRA driver authors who need this can pin their dependency to https://github.com/kubernetes/dynamic-resource-allocation/commit/4361fe437fbafcf2e9cec648d590de43135b3b02.

title: Loss of Kind and APIVersion in Errors from Request.Stream
body:
### What happened?

When invoking the func (r *Request) Stream(ctx context.Context) (io.ReadCloser, error) function in the Kubernetes client-go library, the error returned by the apiserver originally includes fields such as kind and apiVersion (e.g., "kind":"Status","apiVersion":"v1"). However, after passing through the rest-client’s processing logic, these fields (Kind and APIVersion) are stripped from the error object.

This leads to the following issues:

Users lose structured metadata (Kind, APIVersion) from the original server response, which is essential for identifying and categorizing the error type.
It becomes challenging to programmatically distinguish between different error types or versions without additional error handling logic.


### What did you expect to happen?

same as apiserver

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Make a request using the Kubernetes client-go library that results in an error, e.g., an invalid resource request.
Observe the response from the apiserver (e.g., using a network debugging tool like kubectl or other HTTP debugging methods) to verify that the Kind and APIVersion fields are present in the error payload.
Check the error returned by the Request.Stream function to observe the absence of Kind and APIVersion.

### What did you expect to happen?

When a cluster updating to 1.32 from 1.31, we expected (roughly) th same etcd memory usage as 1.31

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Deploy a 1.31 cluster
- upgrade to 1.32
- Observer memory usage on etcd

### Anything else we need to know?

A cluster that was created at v1.32 has an etcd `container_memory_working_set_bytes` of around 130 MB.
A v1.31 cluster is also around 130 MB. After the upgrade to v1.32 it increased to around 450 MB (Caused by a short increase in etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_use_in_bytes to 430 MB). `etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_bytes` permanently increased to 450 MB at upgrade time too. Over time some of the etcds saw an increase in `container_memory_working_set_bytes` to 600MB, but `etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_bytes` did not change.

When it was defragged the `etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_bytes` dropped to 11 MB (Which is just above the value of `etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_use_in_bytes` but `container_memory_working_set_bytes` only dropped to around 450MB.

Once the last v1.31 apiserver has been deleted and replaced by v1.32 apiserver the messages in the v1.32 apiserver logs stop.

(We have 3 apiserver replicas, and they get upgraded 1 by 1, so do have v1.31 & v1.32 apiservers co-existing for a few minutes)

> if old servers are still active, will they duel with a new server to set this key in the configmap?

I can confirm that such a duel indeed occurs :face_exhaling: 

My reproducer:
1. build a `kind` image from master
2. `kind create cluster --config=/home/standa/kind-configs/ha-cluster.yaml --image=kindest/node:latest` - I'll add the config used below
3. `docker exec -ti kind-control-plane sed -i 's#image: .*$#image: registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.31.0#' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` to replace one of the kube-apiservers with an old version.

After kubelet picks up the changes and restarts the KAS, the `kube-system/extension-apiserver-authentication` does get modified in a loop and the new instance loop-logs:
```
I1204 10:37:49.678660       1 cluster_authentication_trust_controller.go:168] writing updated authentication info to  kube-system configmaps/extension-apiserver-authentication
I1204 10:37:49.710061       1 cluster_authentication_trust_controller.go:168] writing updated authentication info to  kube-system configmaps/extension-apiserver-authentication
I1204 10:37:49.730578       1 cluster_authentication_trust_controller.go:168] writing updated authentication info to  kube-system configmaps/extension-apiserver-authentication
I1204 10:37:49.757051       1 cluster_authentication_trust_controller.go:168] writing updated authentication info to  kube-system configmaps/extension-apiserver-authentication
```

I'll have to think a bit on how to fix the issue.

`ha-cluster.yaml`:
```
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
- &control-plane-role
  role: control-plane
  kubeadmConfigPatches:
  - |
    kind: ClusterConfiguration
    apiServer:
        extraArgs:
          v: "2"
- *control-plane-role
- *control-plane-role
```

Our priority is to restore 1.32 to stable behavior as quickly and low risk as possible

The immediate options that come to mind:
1. Full revert
2. Put a feature gate around the surface area (command-line options to add uid headers, publishing uid headers to and consuming uid headers from the configmap) and mark it alpha / disabled by default in 1.32

Then in 1.33 we can work on making the configmap publishing controller tolerate unknown keys so it won't duel, which would make it safe to re-enable in 1.34
Option #2 outlined by Jordan is #129081
Hi folks, we picked up the fix, and confirm we no longer see the issue. Thanks for the speedy resolution 👍

thanks

title: [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Remove ResizePolicy defaulting
body:
/kind bug

Prior to Kubernetes v1.31, any defaulted change to the pod API could trigger running pods to restart on apiserver upgrade (fixed by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124220). Since v1.30 is still within the valid version we cannot set a default ResizePolicy.

Kubelet already handles an unset ResizePolicy as an implicit default (`NotRequired`), so all that is needed here is to remove the defaulting logic. This is probably the preferred behavior even without the version skew issue.

/sig node
/milestone v1.33
/priority important-soon
/triage accepted

### What happened?

According to "https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/build", I use `build/run.sh make test-cmd` to run CLI tests, in my WSL2 environment, and get error: `got error: fork/exec /go/src/k8s.io/kubernetes/_output/local/go/bin/kubeadm: no such file or directory`.

[error-log.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/17686344/error-log.txt)

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/feb3f92bc42f006874f68c476c2d7a6f2ac5ab16/hack/make-rules/test-cmd.sh#L177

`export KUBEADM_PATH="${KUBEADM_PATH:=$(kube::realpath "${KUBE_ROOT}")/_output/dockerized/go/bin/kubeadm}"`, the error is gone.

### What did you expect to happen?

Command `build/run.sh make test-cmd` runs without error: "no such file or directory"

With Docker Desktop, run command `build/run.sh make test-cmd` in WSL2 backend.

title: [Bug] Missing constraint and validation for label selector's values
body:
### What happened?

Hello,
There are some [constraints](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#syntax-and-character-set) that label selector's `values` need to conform:
>* must be 63 characters or less (can be empty),
>* unless empty, must begin and end with an alphanumeric character ([a-z0-9A-Z]),
>* could contain dashes (-), underscores (_), dots (.), and alphanumerics between.

Every label selctor's `values` will be checked [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e5ba5cd2b0d3bddd4a0393b98fde14960f31a33c/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/validation/validation.go#L166C1-L175C2), and when values is not conforming these constraints, an error will be returned.

`nodeAfffinty.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution.nodeSelectorTerms.matchExpressions.values` also needs to conform these constraints (because `matchExpressions` will be parsed as a label selector), but cccording to the [concept documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#operators) and the [API documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.31/#nodeselectorrequirement-v1-core), 
Kubernetes only requires `V1NodeSelectorRequirement.values` to be strings. 
>`values` (string array): An array of string values. If the operator is In or NotIn, the values array must be non-empty. If the operator is Exists or DoesNotExist, the values array must be empty. If the operator is Gt or Lt, the values array must have a single element, which will be interpreted as an integer. This array is replaced during a strategic merge patch.

So when creating a pod with invalid `V1NodeSelectorRequirement.values`, no warning or error message appears and the pod is created successfully.
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: node-affinity-test-pod
  namespace: default
spec:
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
        - matchExpressions:
          - key: int-cmkzofgjsu
            operator: NotIn
            values:
            - '-1' # <- invalid value
  containers:
  - image: nginx
    name: test-container
# pod/node-affinity-test-pod created <- no warning or error here
```
By contrast, when you set an invalid value in matchFields, it will be rejected.
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: node-affinity-test-pod
  namespace: default
spec:
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
        - matchFields:
          - key: metadata.name
            operator: NotIn
            values:
            - '-1'
  containers:
  - image: nginx
    name: test-container
# The Pod "node-affinity-test-pod" is invalid: spec.affinity.nodeAffinity.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution.nodeSelectorTerms[0].matchFields[0].values[0]: Invalid value: "-1": a lowercase RFC 1123 subdomain must consist of lower case alphanumeric characters, '-' or '.', and must start and end with an alphanumeric character (e.g. 'example.com', regex used for validation is '[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?(\.[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?)*')
```
---
And after creating the first pod successfully, it couldn’t be scheduled even though one node satisfied its `nodeAffinity`. By adding some log codes, we found that when the scheduler tries to parse a `nodeSelectorTerm`, it receives a non-empty `parseErr`(because the value is not conforming label value constraints as stated above), causing it to consider the entire `nodeSelectorTerm` unmatched. [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d88b4e3b6e34a85f58778b7ef96e64edffff6823/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/scheduling/corev1/nodeaffinity/nodeaffinity.go#L191C2-L193C3) here.

This behavior may cause the scheduler to make unexpected decisions without the user's awareness. More critically, an invalid value will prevent the entire nodeSelectorTerm from matching.

```yaml
nodeSelectorTerms:
 - matchExpressions:
    - matchExpressions1{key, operator, values} -> has an invalid value, but user is not aware of it
    - matchExpressions2{key, operator, values}
    - ...
   matchFields:
    - matchFields1{key, operator, values}
    - matchFields2{key, operator, values}
    - ...
# matchExpressions1 cannot be parsed, so the whole nodeSelectorTerm is considered as not matched in nodeAffinity
```

### What did you expect to happen?

* Implicit constraints on the [label selector](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/labels/selector.go)'s `values` field should be specified in the API documentation and also validated before creating the pod. (We think not only `nodeAfffinty.requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution.nodeSelectorTerms` will be parsed as label selector, other fields in V1Pod also need to be checked for the same reason.)
* Those implicit constraints should also be added to the concept documentation. (will create an issue in kuberentes/website later)


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Use the yaml file above.

### Anything else we need to know?

/sig bugs scheduling

Tested on 1.30.2

title: iscsi/fc volume with multipath can be incorrectly resolved to partition
body:
### What happened?

If worker nodes are configured so that multipath symlink under `/dev/disk/by-id` points directly to device mapper device (dm-X) the FC/iSCSI volume plugin code in Kubernetes can not handle this well and finds incorrect device.

This is because `FindMultipathDeviceForDevice` function can be called with already resolved symlink and still tries to resolve it further to find its parent - this can resolve in matching a partition of the device, see details below.


If we have a multipath device `scsi-36001405f3392bf76369422cbfd8acd80` pointing to `dm-2`:

```
ls -l /dev/disk/by-id/scsi-36001405f3392bf76369422cbfd8acd80
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 10 Oct 14 14:43 /dev/disk/by-id/scsi-36001405f3392bf76369422cbfd8acd80 -> ../../dm-2
```

This function will try to lookup it's parent, finding `dm-3`:
```
# ls -la /sys/block/dm-3/slaves
total 0
drwxr-xr-x. 2 root root 0 Oct 14 16:29 .
drwxr-xr-x. 9 root root 0 Oct 14 14:43 ..
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 0 Oct 14 14:44 dm-2 -> ../../dm-2
```

Which is actually a partition of the device:
```
# ls -l /dev/disk/by-id/dm-uuid-part1-mpath-36001405f3392bf76369422cbfd8acd80
lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 10 Oct 14 14:43 /dev/disk/by-id/dm-uuid-part1-mpath-36001405f3392bf76369422cbfd8acd80 -> ../../dm-3
```

Multipath and partitions configured:
```
# lsblk
NAME              MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE  MOUNTPOINTS
sda                 8:0    0    50M  0 disk
└─mpathh          253:2    0    50M  0 mpath
  └─mpathh1       253:3    0    10M  0 part
sdb                 8:16   0    50M  0 disk
└─mpathh          253:2    0    50M  0 mpath
  └─mpathh1       253:3    0    10M  0 part
  ...
```

Pod has mounted/attached `253:3` device which is the partition:
```

# lsblk| grep "253:2"
└─mpathh          253:2    0    50M  0 mpath
└─mpathh          253:2    0    50M  0 mpath
```


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Locally with `local-up-cluster.sh`, attaching "fake" loopback device as iSCSI:

- create a loopback device -> `dd if=/dev/zero of=/srv/iscsi/file.img count=102400 && losetup /dev/loop1 /srv/iscsi/file.img`
- partition the loopback device -> `fdisk /dev/loop1`

- discover and attach iSCSI disk to node using both local and loopback IPs to simulate multipath
- enable multipath with `mpathconf --enable --with_multipathd y`
- start local Kubernetes with `local-up-cluster.sh`
- create PV, PVC and Pod:

```

```yaml

spec:

    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50M
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      volumeName: fc-pv-01
```

```yaml

kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: fc-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: busybox
    command: [ "sh", "-c", "sleep infinity" ]
    volumeDevices:
      - name: fc-storage
        devicePath: /dev/data
  volumes:

    persistentVolumeClaim:

title: x509 clients missing User.Uid info for authorization and admission
body:
### What happened?

For all other authenticator types, the authenticator supplies a UID for the user. When an authorizer or admission validator evaluates a request, the uid for x509 users is an empty string.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected a UID to be populated by the x509 authenticator if set in the certificate. I'd also expect `kubeadm` to have a flag in the `kubeadm kubeconfig user` subcommand to support setting it like `--client-name` and `--org` populate username and groups respectively, so something like `--client-uid`. 

For Kubernetes-created node client certs should probably have the node object's `uid`. Other client x509 certs such as Kube-apiserver client cert for node proxy or client certs from the CSR  API, its not clear if/what Kubernetes should set. 



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/) cluster
2. Run `kubectl auth whoami`. No UID is returned as it is for other auth formats

```
kubectl auth whoami
ATTRIBUTE   VALUE
Username    kubernetes-admin
Groups      [kubeadm:cluster-admins system:authenticated]
```


### Anything else we need to know?

As [discussed in #sig-auth](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EN96KUY/p1727984474325949), x509 has an optional field for UID. Go's `crypto/x509` doesn't have a named field for it, but it can be set or accessed.

title: kube-controller-manager re-allocating already used PodCIDR (v1.31)
body:
### What happened?

Since upgrading to Kubernetes v1.31 we have occasional observed that `kube-controller-manager` allocates a PodCIDR for a new node which is already allocated for an existing node in the cluster. We have about 200 clusters with a combined number of ca. 6k-10k nodes (autoscaling). It has happened about 10 times since upgrading a week ago, so it's rather rare but breaks the networking between the affected nodes when it happens.

We use flannel as overlay network and it uses the podCIDR assigned by `kube-controller-manager`. When a new node gets an existing podCIDR assigned, then the new node doesn't get ready and it gets terminated after 10 min. We check that the node is routable by all other nodes before we mark the node ready. This never happens because the podCIDR already points to another node in the cluster. When the new node is deleted it has the very unfortunate side effect that all flannels detect the node is deleted and they delete the routes for the podCIDR, problem is just that most nodes will have routes for the other node with the same podCIDR and this then stops working.

Terminating the affected node is the best way to resolve the issue but obviously not sustainable.

### What did you expect to happen?

`kube-controller-manager` should _never_ allocate the same podCIDR to multiple nodes at the same time.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We haven't found a predictable way to reproduce it.

We run with the pod CIDR range: `10.2.0.0/15`.

### Anything else we need to know?

This is how we configure `kube-controller-manager`: https://github.com/zalando-incubator/kubernetes-on-aws/blob/dev/cluster/node-pools/master-default/userdata.yaml#L581-L648 (the image is vanilla Kubernetes built from source and hosted in a private registry)

Hey I'm back!

I believe I finally understand what is happening.

We are managing the majority of our nodes via [karpenter](https://github.com/aws/karpenter-provider-aws) and it is setting a finalizer on nodes which leads to nodes in this state when being deleted. It can be in this state for a long time if karpenter is stuck draining a node:

```yaml
metadata
  ...
  deletionTimestamp: "2024-10-16T09:54:24Z"
  finalizers:
  - karpenter.sh/termination
```

This particular node was in deletion state for over a day because of a PDB blocking the deletion of a pod.

Looking at the nodeipam controller code it looks like it doesn't consider finalizers when releasing the podCIDR, so it's basically releasing the podCIDR of a still running node and sometimes new nodes happen to get that same podCIDR:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/948afe5ca072329a73c8e79ed5938717a5cb3d21/pkg/controller/nodeipam/ipam/range_allocator.go#L270-L274

It's a bit questionable that karpenter would mark a node for deletion when it had pods with PDBs as it can lead to other problems of a mostly empty node wasting resources, but since this condition is allowed by Kubernetes I think the nodeipam should handle finalizers correctly to not hand out the same podCIDR to multiple nodes.

This is the PR which introduced the change to nodeipam controller: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/123238 this was introduced in v1.31 which explains why we didn't see this issue on v1.30. Before v1.31 the release of CIDR was _only_ done on a node delete event:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/74e84a90c725047b1328ff3d589fedb1cb7a120e/pkg/controller/nodeipam/ipam/range_allocator.go#L161-L163

title: HPA with container metrics fails when any pod is not in a ready state
body:
### What happened?

We've noticed that our HPA will stay at it's current scale and not make decisions when a pod is in an un-Ready state. IE a single pod is in CrashLoopBackoff and the HPA shows:

```
...
resource cpu of container "mycontainer" on pods  (as a percentage of request):     <unknown> / 50%
...
Warning  FailedGetResourceMetric  78s (x7 over 4m7s)  horizontal-pod-autoscaler  unable to get metric cpu: failed to get container metrics: container guides3 not present in metrics for pod namesapce/mycontainer-20240904t1338-433ca6a1-db998df74-s5rfh
```

That particular pod was in CrashLoopBackoff at the time and it wasn't until i removed it was it able to make scaling decisions

We're also running istio so there is another container in these pods and it's running ok; this may be why it's showing up in the metrics but unable to get info on the main container

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect the HPA to ignore pods in this state and use only the Ready pods for its decisions

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Setup an HPA with container based metrics
Put one of the pods in bad state, could just have a single pod consume a lot of memory and have it OOM a few times
See the HPA make no decisions while it's in this state

### Anything else we need to know?

I've looked through the code and it seems to be steming from:
`metrics, err := c.client.PodMetricses(namespace).List(ctx, metav1.ListOptions{LabelSelector: selector.String()})`
This client just uses the selector and doesn't care about the state any of the pods might be in. It does end up filtering out pods later in the reconcile cycle but this returns an error here if it's not in the list of metrics because a single container may not be running 

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.29.6
Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3
Server Version: v1.29.6-gke.1326000
```

</details>

nodes.body: The container metric should come from cadvisor. When an OOM occurs, the container will be deleted and recreated, so HPA may not be able to obtain the container's metrics at this time.

Yeah I understand _why_ it's unable to get metrics but this feels really bad to break the hpa behavior because of a single container; especially one that is in a CrashLoopBackOff state and could get exponentially longer in that state. 


I've seen other instances as well with similar behavior. Another container is on a node that is has memory pressure, gets soft evicted but continues to consume ram, node goes unresponsive and the hpa breaks in a similar way. This single pod not having metrics and in a Terminating state seems line something that should be ignored in favor of the Ready pods, which is what is considered by the end of the reconcile loop

Because this is horizontal expansion, if do not consider these CrashLoopBack pods, the so-called ready pods that are expanded are likely to become CrashLoopBack. Will this lead to the creation of more and more pods, and maybe CrashLoopBack still become ready after the container is rebuilt

If the container's metrics cannot be obtained and the container's status is OOM, is it feasible to treat its memory usage as 100%?

Sure that's half of the equation; in my situation it was scaled to max and unable to scale down even though all metrics of the running pods showed it well under the targets. But even in the Expansion, i'm not sure how adding more pods in a situation like that would cause them to become Crash Loop Back off if you're expanding the pool of pods to take on the workload?

> If the container's metrics cannot be obtained and the container's status is OOM, is it feasible to treat its memory usage as 100%?

Sure if that's what folks agree on. 

I would advocate for treating the returned value much like it does for the Pod metric:
After it gets the metrics in `GetMetricReplicas` we then pass it to `calcPlainMetricReplicas` which takes into consideration the state of the pods and removes them from the calculations 

```
	readyPodCount, unreadyPods, missingPods, ignoredPods := groupPods(podList, metrics, resource, c.cpuInitializationPeriod, c.delayOfInitialReadinessStatus)
	removeMetricsForPods(metrics, ignoredPods)
	removeMetricsForPods(metrics, unreadyPods)
```

instead it just errors out if it's not in the list of metrics found, bubbles up and ends the hpa decision cycle
```
		if !containerFound {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("container %s not present in metrics for pod %s/%s", container, m.Namespace, m.Name)
		}
		
```


If nothing else there should be some doc update to let people know this is the behaviour and how it differs from the Pod metric based HPA calculations
/sig autoscaling
/triage accepted

nodes.title: allow ContainerResource calculations to continue with missing metrics like Resource calculations
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Container metrics based HPA's fail to compute any decision when there is missing metrics for a container within a pod. This can happen when a pod is not in a ready status (has OOM'd or crashed and is in a CrashLoopBackOff, or being terminated and one of the containers has exited and another hasn't etc).
During these windows we should still make decisions in the HPA cycle since we filter out these pods after getting these metrics, currently we just error and exit the loop when this happens

This enables parity between the Pod based metrics and Container based which is what I think most people expect to happen.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #127169

title: Kube-proxy conntrack logic does not consider Service traffic topology
body:
_Originally posted by @adrianmoisey in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126130#issuecomment-2301842312_
            

An UDP Service with internalTrafficPolicy set to Local leaves stale conntrack entries after the endpoint is deleted.

This happens because the Service is deployed as a daemonset with one endpoint per node.

When the endpoint is deleted, the endpoint conntrack entry is deleted but , when the new endpoint is added it should delete the Service ClusterIP entry because the Service effectively went from 0 endpoints in the node (InternalTrafficPolicy Local) to 1 endpoint.

However, the kube-proxy logic to detect stale entries does not have into consideration any of the traffic distribution features for Services, making wrong assumptions because of this and leaving stale entries

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/619b0059cf8c224461cb411fda090c8ff25d9f71/pkg/proxy/endpointschangetracker.go#L290-L350

Kudos to @adrianmoisey for the thorough investigation and reproducer

/sig network
/kind bug
/assign @aojea

I can not repro with the e2e test in this release or previous https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/126935

however, I can do it with kind in 1.29 version locally .... checking more into this

cc: @danwinship

Talked with @danwinship offline, he explained that in recent versions a DROP rule was added, so that rule can cause that the conntrack entry is not created.

We need to merge the information from both the Services and EndpointSlices cache to be able to include the `CategorizeEndpoint()`  logic to figure out the actual Endpoints and Services that are programmed in the dataplane , so we can detect the entries that may be stale.

Since he is more familiar with the codebase of the endpointslice and service caches, I'm reassigning this to him

/assign @danwinship

@danwinship since @aroradaman is working on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126130 this cycle that will allow us to no longer depend on the cache logic for conntrack deletion, I wonder if we just can have a backportable change that fixes the issue in the supported minor versions and avoid any refactor

OK, so the behavior that we _want_ here is

- When a service goes from 0 endpoints to non-0 endpoints on this node, delete all blackhole conntrack entries for the service's IPs.

The behavior we currently have is:

- When a service goes from 0 endpoints to non-0 endpoints **~on this node~**, delete all **~blackhole~** conntrack entries for the service's IPs.

Using netlink doesn't help with the endpoint-counting part, but if the netlink filter is able to distinguish blackhole entries from non-blackhole entries, then we could change the rule to be:

- Any time a service's endpoints change, delete all blackhole conntrack entries for the service's IPs.

or slightly more efficiently:

- When a service goes from 0 endpoints to non-0 endpoints, _or_ any time the service's endpoints change if the service has Local traffic policy or uses topology, then delete all blackhole conntrack entries for the service's IPs.

But long term, fixing the endpoint counting is probably still the right fix.

> I wonder if we just can have a backportable change that fixes the issue in the supported minor versions and avoid any refactor

Are you suggesting backporting the netlink conntrack code? That seems like a pretty big backport...

> Are you suggesting backporting the netlink conntrack code? That seems like a pretty big backport...

no, sorry, I;m saying that if we have the reconciler in  place in this release, the conntrack delete logic is different, we look at the existing services, we look at the existing conntrack entries and we delete the ones that does not match ... we no longer depend on the heuristics of if service had ... and now has ... and this happened ...

But we still depend on that for the old releases, I'm not in favor of backporting the reconciler not even the netlink thing, is very risky, what I was trying to understand is if we can get a patch that fixes the problem without having to refactor too mach so we can backport it

Oh, you mean, if we get the reconciler in 1.32 but _don't_ have the topology fix in 1.32, can we later do the topology fix in a way that could be backported to 1.32?

If we are changing conntrack cleanup to be primarily based on reconciliation, then we have to totally change how the proxiers interact with the conntrack cleanup code anyway, so we should fix the topology bug at the same time. If we don't fix it then, then I don't think the eventual future fix is likely to be any more backport-able with the reconciler than it would be with the existing code. (The problem here is not with the "if service had ... and now has ... and this happened" part, it's that we're looking at the wrong data when we decide what to do. As soon as we fix it to pass the right data to the conntrack code, the problem fixes itself.)

> f we get the reconciler in 1.32 but _don't_ have the topology fix in 1.32, can we later do the topology fix in a way that could be backported to 1.32?

I was asking if we can get the topology fix before the reconciler change ... so we can backport it

> . As soon as we fix it to pass the right data to the conntrack code, the problem fixes itself.

yeah, that is the part when I gave up and asked you for help 😄  , every possible solution I came up was really hacky

I think, at the point where we currently call

    endpointUpdateResult := proxier.endpointsMap.Update(proxier.endpointsChanges)

we need to change things so that the `CategorizeEndpoints` step happens then too, and is reflected in `endpointsMap` (or whatever `endpointsMap` becomes).

We need to do that _here_ because if we don't, then that implies we will essentially have to create a duplicate copy of `endpointsMap` with slightly different data later on for use by the conntrack reconciler, and we don't want to do that because the endpoint state is potentially enormous.

Two other things feeding into the refactoring:
- #112604 points out that we need to be able to roll back the effect of `proxier.endpointsMap.Update()` above if the sync fails. Right now `EndpointsTracker` keeps track of the currently-committed endpoint state, and any pending un-synced changes, but we need to make it keep track of 3 states (committed, currently-attempting-to-commit, and pending) instead. That also implies a more complicated `endpointsMap` representation, because we don't want to have to keep the old `endpointsMap` around to be able to roll back to it.
- #126013 effectively _did_ add a duplicate copy of `endpointsMap` to use for figuring out nftables partial syncs, because the existing tracker/map APIs don't expose diffs, only the final state. We need to add tracker/map APIs to be able to determine the diff between the "committed" and "currently-attempting-to-commit" states.

Anyway, I'm thinking about how to make this all work nicely...
Should we close this one?, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127318 handles this as well.

> Should we close this one?, #127318 handles this as well.

Thanks for finding this
/Close

Ah... I was thinking [before](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126934#issuecomment-2334233202) that the reconciler wouldn't fix this, because it _wouldn't_ fix it if we had kept the same logic as the old cleanup code. But using the netlink API lets us do a better job of cleaning things correctly than we did before, and Daman took advantage of that, so this bug is fixed too.

> When the endpoint is deleted, the endpoint conntrack entry is deleted but , when the new endpoint is added it should delete the Service ClusterIP entry because the Service effectively went from 0 endpoints in the node (InternalTrafficPolicy Local) to 1 endpoint.
> 
> However, the kube-proxy logic to detect stale entries does not have into consideration any of the traffic distribution features for Services, making wrong assumptions because of this and leaving stale entries

The new reconciler just correctly deletes all of the conntrack entries for the deleted endpoint at the point that the endpoint gets deleted, so it doesn't need an extra hack for "the number of endpoints went from 0 to 1", so it doesn't need to care about the distinction between globally-relevant and locally-relevant endpoints.
Amazing, thanks everyone. When we upgrade to 1.32, I'll give this a try.

title: Ignore and potentially prevent reporting container status for not-existing containers

title: No ICMP is received when connecting to a node without local PODs when externalTrafficPolicy:Local is used
body:
### What happened?

Due to following upstream changes (K8s commit): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/97081, when there is no local endpoint then kube-proxy will route the traffic to other endpoints in the cluster.

This change is added to support use-case/issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/92857, where a POD within the cluster should be able to access the service by External LB IP. But this is causing an issue:

When a node ~~(which is not hosting any local endpoint)~~ (whose local endpoint is restarted and currently not up) receives traffic that is sent from an external IP to service LB IPreceives traffic that is sent from an external IP to service LB IP, the traffic is not SNATed as the service `ExternalTrafficPolicy` is 'local' but the traffic is forwarded to other node, resulting it to be dropped by other node. Thus connection remains `UNREPLIED` in conntrack.

This is breaking following use-case:

When we upgrade the deployment/daemonset, as the local end-points are going down and coming up again with new changes, for some time during this operation kube-proxy updates ipvs to forward traffic to other endpoints.

During this time any midstream redirected traffic causes conntrack entry to be as ESTABLISHED - UNREPLIED, and for any new connection it causes conntrack to register it as SYN-SENT - UNREPLIED
 
This causes significant traffic drop (blackholing) until this entry gets flushed out from conntrack.

### What did you expect to happen?

No traffic loss.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy kubernetes cluster, with at least two worker nodes
2. Set `kube-proxy` mode to `ipvs`
3. Create a following daemonset:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  labels:
    app: debugger-ds
  name: debugger-ds
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: debugger-ds
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: debugger-ds
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: ealen/echo-server:0.7.0
        name: http-https-echo
      initContainers:
      - name: init-nginx
        image: nginx:latest
        command: ['sleep', '120']

```
3. Create a LoadBalancer Service

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  labels:
    app: debugger-ds
  name: dubugger-svc
spec:
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  ipFamilies:
  - IPv4
  ipFamilyPolicy: SingleStack
  ports:
  - name: debug-port
    port: 80
    targetPort: 80
  selector:
    app: debugger-ds
  type: LoadBalancer
```
4.  Set a static route from external server to one of the workers(worker-2).
5. Run hping3 command from external server to establish tcp connection to a worker-2. It is important to specify the source port here. 

`sudo hping3 -i u10000 -s <FIXED_SRC_PORT> --keep -p <SVC_PORT> -S <SVC_EXT_IP>
`
 6. Delete debugger-ds pod from worker-2. 

We can see tcp   UNREPLIED conntrack entries on worker-2. 
`
6 119 SYN_SENT src=192.168.39.1 dst=192.168.0.12 sport=40100 dport=80 [UNREPLIED] src=10.244.2.7 dst=192.168.39.1 sport=80 dport=40100 mark=0 use=1`


 

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

`Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"25", GitVersion:"v1.25.3", GitCommit:"434bfd82814af038ad94d62ebe59b133fcb50506", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-10-12T10:49:09Z", GoVersion:"go1.19.2", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}`

> When a node (which is not hosting any local endpoint) receives traffic that is sent from an external IP to service LB IP, the traffic is not SNATed as the service ExternalTrafficPolicy is 'local' but the traffic is forwarded to other node,

why the node will receive that traffic in the first instance if does not have any pod there? that is why we have healtcheck nodeports, to indicate the external. loadbalancers to not forward traffic there

Is this a duplicate of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113203?
/assign @uablrek @aojea

> > When a node (which is not hosting any local endpoint) receives traffic that is sent from an external IP to service LB IP, the traffic is not SNATed as the service ExternalTrafficPolicy is 'local' but the traffic is forwarded to other node,
> 
> why the node will receive that traffic in the first instance if does not have any pod there? that is why we have healtcheck nodeports, to indicate the external. loadbalancers to not forward traffic there
> 
> Is this a duplicate of #113203?

Sorry for the confusion, I updated the issue.

I can reproduce the UNREPLIED conntrack entry, but not the problem. I use a DaemonSet with `nodeSelector`, so I can control where the PODs are started, and static routes for the loadBalancerIP. The UNREPLIED can easily be created as:

1. Set a static route to a node where the POD is **not** running
2. Try a TCP connect (or use hping3, it doesn't matter)

On the node that is target for the static route an UNREPLIED conntrack entry is created as described in this issue:

```
tcp      6 119 SYN_SENT src=192.168.1.201 dst=10.0.0.0 sport=7000 dport=5001 [UNREPLIED] src=11.0.2.2 dst=192.168.1.201 sport=5001 dport=7000 mark=0 use=1
```
But when a POD (endpoint) is later started on that node, the UNREPLIED entry is erased and the TCP connect is succesful (no blackholing).

```
tcp      6 431991 ESTABLISHED src=192.168.1.201 dst=10.0.0.0 sport=7000 dport=5001 src=11.0.3.2 dst=192.168.1.201 sport=5001 dport=7000 [ASSURED] mark=0 use=1
```
Please note that a fixed source port (7000) is used.
There has been corrections in the kernel for conntrack, so this _may_ be kernel version dependent. @aojea may know more about that. I am using `linux-6.3.4`.

yep https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113203#issuecomment-1287313833

https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/e15d4cdf27cb0c1e977270270b2cea12e0955edd

@Sunnatillo Can you please check if the UNREPLIED conntrack remains even after a local POD is started as described in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/119131#issuecomment-1625290063? And when using a recent kernel.

Note that packets routed to a node without a POD are replied, but with a POD-ip as source, described in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/93456#issuecomment-733069629. Please check if that can cause any problems outside K8s in your setup (it shouldn't really)

Hi @uablrek 
Commenting on behalf of @Sunnatillo. In our setup we see packets are forwarded to node with server, VIP replaced with POD-IP. We see no response packets. I see packets got dropped actually before reaching the destination POD-IP.

We see no issues with traffic generated within cluster to same VIP/LB-IP.

As their is no reset or ICMP destination unreachable sent to external client the connection is hung. This is an issue for us. Can this be fixed such that if src IP or client IP is outside the cluster then connection is terminated soon?

Once POD is UP in the target node we see ipvsadm entry for fwd node endpoint IP got removed and UNREPLIED conntrack entry too removed.

Ok, I see. This problem has _nothing to do with conntrack, nor the choice of source port_. The title should be something like:

"No ICMP is received when connecting to a node without local PODs when externalTrafficPolicy:Local is used"

In K8s <v1.24 (without the PR) "ICMP Port Unreachable" was sent from the node where no local PODs exist. This because there were no "real servers" configured in ipvs.

In K8s >=v1.24 the remote endpoints are configured as "real servers" and packets are eventually dropped without an ICMP (black holed). A program that call connect(2) will timeout after a "default" time that seem to vary, but some searching gives that it is ~75s for Windows and Linux. When a POD is started on the node _or_ the (faulty) route to a node without local POD is corrected, then the program hanging on connect(2) will connect successfully.

IMO this is not a bug in K8s, but a normal case any networking program must handle. But it is a changed behavior, so I set

/triage accepted

The [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/97081) does however fix a real bug in K8s that makes e2e tests fail.

Whenever this should be fixed or not, I leave to discussion.

@uablrek I'm not quite grasping it yet, could you please explain bit more about "program handling" part. In this case, the traffic forwarded from a node A(where pod not exist) to a node B(where pod exists), dropped when reaching the node B and did not reach the pod.

Yes, that's intentional for _external traffic_. Traffic that originates from an external source that is. For _internal traffic_, in this case from a POD without hostNetwork:true, the traffic should be directed to a POD on another node, with the (POD) source address intact.

Hi @uablrek 
Above comment seems to be fine for new connection. For mid stream redirected packets coming to a node where local endpoint goes down, conntrack entry gets created with ESTABLISHED UNREPLIED (5 min timer) state.
Once local endpoint comes up again the connection with same 5 tuple will continue to be dropped and the above mentioned kernel/conntrack fix is not applicable to established conntrack entries. Thus timer keeps on refreshing until we keep on receiving the traffic from client.

I think if we get TCP Reset/ICMP port unreachable(as before) then client side connection will be terminated quickly. Currently client has to wait for TCP timer to expire.

> Yes, that's intentional for _external traffic_. Traffic that originates from an external source that is. For _internal traffic_, in this case from a POD without hostNetwork:true, the traffic should be directed to a POD on another node, with the (POD) source address intact.

If an `eTP: Local` lb-address (EXTERNAL IP) is accessed from a POD on the local cluster, it counts as internal traffic and is directed to a POD on another node if no local pod exist. The contract; _the original source it preserved_, is still honored since it's an internal pod address.
However, that _is_ a special case, and the implementation in proxy-mode=ipvs is particularly... odd. _IMO this issue can be closed_ with a recommendation to switch to proxy-mode=nftables.
The icmp-or-no-icmp question has been debated, and as I recall the conclusion is **no-icmp**. The reason is that this normally happens in during a re-configuration, and the re-try SYN will succeed. To send an icmp may fool a client to assume the server to be unreachable.

title: Forbidden accessing or modifying other pod's cgroup in privileged container
body:
### What happened?

I created a `privileged` pod on K8S v1.24.0. Use `kubectl exec` to enter the pod's shell, i noticed that the whole host cgroupfs was mount at `/sys/fs/cgroup` with `rw` mode. And i can get other pod's cgroup, even modify it!

Created `privileged` pod on K8S v1.25.2, same results. Created `privileged` pod on K8S v1.22.0 and v1.23.0, i can only access and modify the cgroup of the current pod, which is what i expect.

BTW, my OS is ubuntu-22.04 (kernel v5.15.0) with cgroup v2. When i tested in ubuntu-18.04 (kernel v4.15.0) with cgroup v1, K8S v1.24.0/v1.25.2/v1.23.0/v1.22.0 worked as expect!

### What did you expect to happen?

Forbidden accessing or modifying other pod's cgroup in privileged pod on K8S v1.24.0 (or higher).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

step1. Use OS ubuntu-22.04 (or other distributions with cgroup v2)
step2. Create K8S cluster v1.24.0 (or higher) by kubeadm (follow the doc [kubeadm)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/production-environment/tools/kubeadm/install-kubeadm/#installing-runtime)
step3. Install CNI plugin (i use calico)
step4. Create a privileged pod use the below manifest, and discover its `/sys/fs/cgroup`

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: alpine
spec:
  containers:
  - image: alpine
    name: alpine
    command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
    securityContext:
      privileged: true
```

title: Exclusive CPUs not removed from deleted Pod and put back in the defaultCPUSet.
body:
### What happened?

The `CPUManager` has logic to periodically cleanup stale state and reclaim exclusive CPUs from pods that have recently terminated. It does this by querying the system for a list of `activePods()` and reclaiming CPUs from any pods it is tracking that are not in this list.

This works fine for most pods, but special care needs to be taken to ensure that CPUs are not accidentally reclaimed from pods that have not started yet. Allocation of CPUs to the containers of a pod happens during pod admission (i.e. before the pod is added to the `activePods()` list), so a simple state variable (`pendingAdmissionPod`) is used to indicate which pod is currently being admitted and exclude it from cleanup. Since pod admission is serialized, only one pod will ever be pending admission at a given time, and only a single variable is necessary to track this (i.e. whenever a new pod enters the admission loop to have exclusive CPUs granted to it, `pendingAdmissionPod` is overwritten to point to the new pod, clearing way for the previous one to have its state cleaned up when appropriate).

Unfortunately, this simple procedure can cause problems because `pendingAdmissionPod` is never reset to `nil` after the **last** pod is admitted. This is usually fine, because the next time a pod comes in for admission, it will be overwritten to point to the new pod. But if no new pods come in, then it continues to point to the last pod that we attempted to admit (forever essentially), making it so that we can never cleanup its state if it gets deleted at some point in the future (because it is always treated as an "active" pod so long as it is pointed to by `pendingAdmissionPod`).

I don't think this issue is critical, since in any practical setting pods will be started and stopped all the time, clearing way for the state of previously admitted pods to be cleaned up. But we should consider a better method of tracking pods that are `notYetActiveButPendingAdmission()` so that we can eliminate this weird edge case.

### What did you expect to happen?

With `--cpu-manager-policy=static` enabled on a node.

Look at the CPU set assigned to one of the system pods running on that node in a non-Guaranteed QOS class:
```
$ kubectl exec -it <pod> -- taskset -cp 1
pid 1's current affinity list: 0-255
```

Create a pod requesting exclusive CPUs:
```
$ cat pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-pod
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - image: ubuntu:20.04
    name: test-ctr
    command: ["bash", "-c"]
    args: ["sleep 99999"]
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 4000m
        memory: 1Gi
```
```
$ kubectl apply -f pod.yml
pod/test-pod created
```

Look at the set of exclusive CPUs granted to it (we should see 4):
```
$ kubectl exec -it test-pod -- taskset -cp 1
pid 1's current affinity list: 1,2,129,130
```

Look again at the set of CPU set assigned to the pod in the non-Guaranteed QOS class (the 4 CPUs from above are gone):
```
$ kubectl exec -it <pod> -- taskset -cp 1
pid 1's current affinity list: 0,3-128,131-255
```

Delete the test pod:
```
$ kubectl delete pod test-pod
pod "test-pod" deleted
```

Look again at the set of CPU set assigned to the pod in the non-Guaranteed QOS class (we are back to the original set):
```
$ kubectl exec -it <pod> -- taskset -cp 1
pid 1's current affinity list: 0-255
```

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Go through the steps above, but the last step doesn't show the original CPU set restored.
```
$ kubectl exec -it <pod> -- taskset -cp 1
pid 1's current affinity list: 0,3-128,131-255
```

### Anything else we need to know?

title: exec over web sockets protocol is flawed
body:
**What happened**:
I tried to use exec over web sockets (as implemented in the C# Kubernetes client), but the protocol does not seem to have a way to communicate when STDIN is closed. This causes commands to run forever if they wait for STDIN to be closed, and is especially bad when the command won't send its output until then.

**What you expected to happen**:
I expect the exec protocol to have a mechanism to communicate when STDIN is closed, since this is important for the execution of many commands. The SPDY implementation has such a mechanism. (IIRC, a serious bug in SPDY exec v1 - documented in v1.go - was a similar lack of detection for closing STDIN.)

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
Exec /bin/cat (without arguments) over web sockets. Send some data and try to close STDIN while receiving all of the output.

**Anything else we need to know?**:
You can force the command to terminate by half-closing the web socket connection, but this is not a solution because Kubernetes interprets it as "close the connection ASAP" rather than "finish running the command, send all the output, and close the connection". This may cause the output to be truncated.

The core web socket handler code seems to be this:

    // handle implements a websocket handler.
    func (conn *Conn) handle(ws *websocket.Conn) {
          defer conn.Close()
          conn.initialize(ws)
    
          for {
                conn.resetTimeout()
                var data []byte
                if err := websocket.Message.Receive(ws, &data); err != nil {
                      if err != io.EOF {
                            klog.Errorf("Error on socket receive: %v", err)
                      }
                      break
                }
                if len(data) == 0 {
                      continue
                }
                channel := data[0]
                if conn.codec == base64Codec {
                      channel = channel - '0'
                }
                data = data[1:]
                if int(channel) >= len(conn.channels) {
                      klog.V(6).Infof("Frame is targeted for a reader %d that is not valid, possible protocol error", channel)
                      continue
                }
                if _, err := conn.channels[channel].DataFromSocket(data); err != nil {
                      klog.Errorf("Unable to write frame to %d: %v\n%s", channel, err, string(data))
                      continue
                }
          }
    }

As you can see, it skips zero-byte messages, takes the channel from the first byte, and sends the remaining data to the channel. There is no provision for closing STDIN, nor does there seem to be anything in the implementation of DataFromSocket that would do it, as far as I can see.

My suggestions on how to fix it are:

1. Use the web sockets "finish" flag to mark the end of STDIN. The client would set "finish" to true on the last STDIN frame. This is more or less what the finish flag was designed for.
2. Make half-closing the web socket equivalent to closing STDIN. Kubernetes should finish executing the command normally, send all the output, and then close its side of the connection. Kubernetes can reserve the "abort the command" behavior for the client performing a full close of the connection.
2. Or, interpret an empty web sockets message as an end-of-stream marker for STDIN. Since empty messages are not allowed - all messages are supposed to be prefixed with the channel ID - this shouldn't be a breaking change in protocol.

The first seems quite proper, but unfortunately, the websocket library Kubernetes uses doesn't seem to expose the flag. The second also seems fairly proper, but may also have difficulties in implementation. The third seems easy to implement.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"17", GitVersion:"v1.17.3", GitCommit:"06ad960bfd03b39c8310aaf92d1e7c12ce618213", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2020-02-11T18:14:22Z", GoVersion:"go1.13.6", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"14", GitVersion:"v1.14.2", GitCommit:"66049e3b21efe110454d67df4fa62b08ea79a19b", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2019-05-16T16:14:56Z", GoVersion:"go1.12.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"}

- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: Azure VM

- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`):
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION="16.04.6 LTS (Xenial Xerus)"
ID=ubuntu
ID_LIKE=debian
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 16.04.6 LTS"
VERSION_ID="16.04"
HOME_URL="http://www.ubuntu.com/"
SUPPORT_URL="http://help.ubuntu.com/"
BUG_REPORT_URL="http://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/"
VERSION_CODENAME=xenial
UBUNTU_CODENAME=xenial

- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): Linux AdamArisDev 4.15.0-1063-azure #68-Ubuntu SMP Fri Nov 8 09:30:20 UTC 2019 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux

- Others:
My cluster is running in minikube v1.1.0.

I just ran into this very issue attempting to create a better python client integration with the pod exec api over web sockets. There is no way to communicate to the exec'ed process that stdin has closed.
/remove-lifecycle stale

At the moment the SPDY implementation's `Close()` method on a stream (not connection) does a half-close. I think we need a way to do that rather than using an empty message to mean "close stdin" channel. What if in the future we'll need more than a single writable channel for some purpose, not only stdin?

What if we introduce a v5 protocol and treat messages with channel id only as a half-close signal? That would match SPDY and seems like a clean, easy, and backwards compatible solution.

WDYT?

One more thing a new protocol needs to support is resetting a steam - meaning no data should be sent by both parties and anything received should be discarded.

Edit: Maybe we can use the highest bit of the channel id as a marker to distinguish between control vs normal messages and then control messages body can contain control information such as `0` meaning `half-close the channel`, `1` `reset the channel`. Something like that? Alternatively, we can use a special value, such as 0xFF for the control messages. After it, body contains channel number byte and then the rest is as above. That way we only reduce the max number of channels by 1 rather than by half (127).

Actually, if we take the control channel approach, then how will a server of an older version react? Will we need a new protocol version in that case (i.e. if it just discards messages for unknown channels then we don't need new protocol)? Need to investigate the server side.

title: TOB-K8S-033: Services use questionable default functions
body:
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/wg-security-audit/findings/Kubernetes%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Description**
Many services in Kubernetes use questionable default functions, such as insecure random number generation or dangerous temporary file creation.

In regards to random number generation, many services, including kubelet, api-server, kube-scheduler, kube-proxy, seed the random number generator in the following manner.

```
rand.Seed(time.Now().UnixNano())
```
Figure 27.1: The common method of seeding rand with time in Kubernetes.

Generally this is okay. The code properly uses crypto/rand for cryptographic operations like key generations. No cryptographic primitives were observed incorrectly using math/rand.

However, due to this seeding, certain identifiers are predictable and simplify aspects of an exploitation chain. In Figure 33.2, the node is assigned a random name that could be guessable to an attacker who knows uptime information.

```
func (kubemarkController *KubemarkController) addNodeToNodeGroup(nodeGroup string) error {
	node := kubemarkController.nodeTemplate.DeepCopy()
        ...
	node.Name = fmt.Sprintf("%s-%d", nodeGroup, kubemarkController.rand.Int63())
        ...
        client.CoreV1().ReplicationControllers(node.Namespace).Create(node)
}
```
Figure 27.2: An example of using time-seeded values to add a node to a group.

Another concerning function was found in the kubectl create --edit command, which creates a temporary file to edit objects before creation. This temporary file is created via a custom tempFile function (Figure 33.3) called by LaunchTempFile (Figure 33.4). It is possible to create all possible temporary files that would be used, leading to the kubectl create --edit command to fail.

There is also a potential race condition in LaunchTempFile between closing the file and opening it later in the editor. However, since the file is created with 0600 permissions, this appears to be a non-issue.

```
func tempFile(prefix, suffix string) (f *os.File, err error) {
	dir := os.TempDir()

	for i := 0; i < 10000; i++ {
		name := filepath.Join(dir, prefix+randSeq(5)+suffix)
		f, err = os.OpenFile(name, os.O_RDWR|os.O_CREATE|os.O_EXCL, 0600)
		if os.IsExist(err) {
			continue
		}
		break
	}
	return
}
```
Figure 27.3: The tempFile function definition.

```
func (e Editor) LaunchTempFile(prefix, suffix string, r io.Reader) ([]byte, string, error) {
	f, err := tempFile(prefix, suffix)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, "", err
	}
	defer f.Close()
	path := f.Name()
	if _, err := io.Copy(f, r); err != nil {
		os.Remove(path)
		return nil, path, err
	}
	// This file descriptor needs to close so the next process (Launch) can claim it.
	f.Close()
	if err := e.Launch(path); err != nil {
		return nil, path, err
	}
	bytes, err := ioutil.ReadFile(path)
	return bytes, path, err
}
```
Figure 27.4: The LaunchTempFile function definition.

**Exploit Scenario**
If an attacker needs to know the name or identifier of a service, Pod, or node that is infeasible to brute force, the attacker may be able to deduce the uptime from the current environment and enumerate possible seeds, narrowing the space of possible names and identifiers.

Regarding the tempFile, the attacker can create all possible temporary files (36**5 = 60466176), preventing the kubectl create --edit from creating the temporary file.

**Recommendation**
Short term, seed the random number generator using a less predictable seed.

Long term, investigate whether the standard library ioutil.TempFile function would be a viable replacement for the current tempFile implementation. Ensure appropriate use of math/rand and crypto/rand, and ensure correct random number generator seeding.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

See #81146 for current status of all issues created from these findings.

The vendor gave this issue an ID of TOB-K8S-033 and it was finding 30 of the report.

The vendor considers this issue Low Severity.

To view the original finding, begin on page 75 of the [Kubernetes Security Review Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/wg-security-audit/findings/Kubernetes%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Environment**:

- Kubernetes version: 1.13.4

title: TOB-K8S-021: Improper fetching of PIDs allows incorrect cgroup movement
body:
This issue was reported in the [Kubernetes Security Audit Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/wg-security-audit/findings/Kubernetes%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Description**
Kubelet fetches a process’s PID by checking the process name when the pidfile file doesn’t exist. This fallback mechanism doesn’t validate the target process allowing an attacker to spoof it.

Kubelet’s container manager first tries to use a hardcoded pidfile path to retrieve the PIDs of important processes, like dockerd and docker-containerd (Figure 1).

```
const (
	// (...)
	dockerProcessName     = "docker"
	dockerPidFile         = "/var/run/docker.pid"
	containerdProcessName = "docker-containerd"
	containerdPidFile     = "/run/docker/libcontainerd/docker-containerd.pid"
)
```
Figure 16.1: Hardcoded pidfiles paths.

If these hard-coded files do not exist, then the container manager will fall back to scanning `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`. If the pidfile is not there, and this happens to be the case on our setup, an attacker may move an unprivileged, cgroups-limited process on the host to manager’s cgroup and set its OOM-killer badness heuristic to -999, making the process less likely to be killed in out-of-memory scenarios.

**Exploit Scenario**
Alice has kubelet running on a machine where the docker-containerd pidfile is located in a different path than the hardcoded one. Eve gains access to Alice’s machine and notices kubelet is running. Eve’s current cgroup limits her too much for what she is attempting to perform on the machine, so she uses kubelet’s cgroup monitoring to migrate her process into an elevated cgroup.

Eve can execute the attack by simply renaming her malicious process to docker-containerd, launching it and waiting five minutes (so kubelet moves it to the cgroup and sets the OOM-killer badness heuristic).

**Recommendation**
Use only pidfiles and let users configure paths to them. This relates to issue #34066. If enforcing the use of pidfiles only is not an option, consider adding checks to identify whether given PID is really the targeted process and warn users that the pidfile hasn’t been found.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

See #81146 for current status of all issues created from these findings.

The vendor gave this issue an ID of TOB-K8S-021 and it was finding 16 of the report.

The vendor considers this issue Medium Severity.

To view the original finding, begin on page 50 of the [Kubernetes Security Review Report](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/wg-security-audit/findings/Kubernetes%20Final%20Report.pdf)

**Environment**:

- Kubernetes version: 1.13.4
